articles.title_orig: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
articles.title_zh: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
articles.content_orig:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda , Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Tsunami alert issued in the Tyrrhenian Sea after 2 earthquakes rock Palermo, Italy
articles.title_zh: Tsunami alert issued in the Tyrrhenian Sea after 2 earthquakes rock Palermo, Italy
articles.content_orig:
While you may think quakes are a western US problem, some of the largest temblors in US history have happened in the East.
PALERMO, Italy — Palermo, the capital of Sicily, and other cities in southern Italy were rocked by a series of earthquakes in the Tyrrhenian Sea on Friday, including a magnitude 5.7 quake, according to USGS.
Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology has recorded nearly three dozen earthquakes, most of them weaker, in the same area of the southern Tyrrhenian Sea north of Sicily.
View of Palermo, Sicily, Italy, Europe.
(Mauro Flamini/REDA/Universal Images Group via Getty Images / Getty Images)
A magnitude 4.9 quake struck just before noon local time Friday, followed by the magnitude 5.7 quake around 12:20 p.m, according to the USGS.
The epicenters of both quakes were about 6 miles below the surface.
A magnitude 5.2 quake struck just before 4 p.m. about 30 miles west-northwest of Malfa.
(FOX Weather / FOX Weather)
The Palermo government said the mayor is expected to sign an order ordering the evacuation of some public buildings and people were urged to stay out of the water and avoid boating.
The city government of Bagheria said first responders are conducting building inspections and local schools were evacuated. Italy’s national tsunami warning system issued tsunami alerts for coastal areas around Bagheria, the city said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Volvo Shares Plunge as China Ambitions Fade for Western Carmakers
articles.title_zh: Volvo Shares Plunge as China Ambitions Fade for Western Carmakers
articles.content_orig:
Volvo Cars said Friday it plans to cut 2,500 jobs after a sharp decline in its Chinese market weighed on third-quarter earnings.
The Swedish automaker reported an operating loss of 5.6 billion Swedish kronor ($563.7 million) in the third quarter, down from an operating profit of 6.4 billion Swedish kronor in the previous period.
The company, which is owned by China's Geely Holding, cited a deteriorating environment led by "tougher" market conditions in China and the U.S., which "negatively affected free cash flow."
Volvo Cars shares were 24.2% lower at the end of the trading session.
"It's really a lot about the Chinese market, of course, where the change has come faster than we thought, and really now we can see that selling global cars developed in Europe and China will not work, and then this is affecting all the Western players in China," Volvo Cars CEO Håkan Samuelsson told CNBC on "Squawk Box Europe," on Friday.
Chinese consumers are now looking for "domestic alternatives," which have become stronger and more competitive, the CEO said. "We need a new strategy in China... it has to be a more regional structure, a more empowered region, and we need regionally adapted cars."
He added that costs must be competitive and that Volvo Cars needs to share some platforms with its Chinese parent company Geely, and develop key software in China that includes infotainment and driver-assistance systems. "If you don't have that, I think you cannot sell cars in China."
Volvo Cars' revenues in China fell almost 50% year-on-year as premium brands faced "hypercompetition" from new Chinese rivals, which also put severe pressure on pricing, the company said.
Meanwhile, in the U.S., the automaker cited negative effects from tariffs and fewer customer incentives to buy electric cars, putting pressure on profit margins.
Volvo Cars said it is looking to cut 5 billion Swedish kronor in costs and will eliminate 2,500 jobs globally, with 2,000 of those jobs based in Sweden.
"It is really a consequence of this development, our long-range strategy," Samuelsson told CNBC. "We will have more empowered, stronger regions, and then of course you cannot keep the same resources on the corporate central level. So we need a leaner central administration."

China’s domestic online beauty sales are falling as C-beauty companies are ramping up export efforts and moving into international retail channels. The gap suggests a deliberate pivot from C-beauty toward overseas growth, targeting the categories and regions that K-beauty has spent the past decade winning over.
According to Jefferies’ China online beauty tracker , the country recorded a 6% year-on-year cosmetics sales decline in September 2026. Skin care fell 6.1%, while color cosmetics went down 5.2%.
However, at the same time, data from the Korea International Trade Association (KITA) shows China climbing from seventh place to fifth in global cosmetics exports. The trade body says China’s color cosmetics exports amount to nearly three times that of Korea’s.
C-beauty company Proya, meanwhile, has opened a European Innovation Center Laboratory in France and has announced it will begin selling across 400 Ulta Beauty stores in the US next month.
“This Europe Innovation Center Laboratory connects the European and Chinese ecosystems to draw on combined strengths and create new innovation capabilities,” says Hou Juncheng, founder and chairman of Proya Cosmetics.
The center is not the first bridge between Chinese and European beauty. French ingredient suppliers have been actively pursuing partnerships with Chinese cosmetics brands, and many Chinese perfumers train in France. The country’s Cosmetic Valley, meanwhile, has set up a Shanghai-based fragrance and cosmetics embassy to encourage collaboration between the two markets . Chinese beauty brands are expanding overseas, targeting markets where K-beauty has established a strong presence.
With color cosmetics exports already outpacing Korea’s and a growing foothold in US and European retail, C-beauty appears to be borrowing the playbook that got K-beauty onto global shelves.
The September figures from Jefferies’ tracker show many multinational beauty giants experiencing declining figures in China. L’Oréal fell 5%, Estée Lauder 8%, Procter & Gamble 20%, Shiseido 24%, and LVMH 26%.
Beiersdorf and Galderma were the only multinationals to grow, supported by their Nivea and Cetaphil brands. At the brand level, dermatological skin care like CeraVe and Cetaphil grew (35% and 58%, respectively), while Bobbi Brown fell 31%. Among domestic players, Mao Geping grew 26%, and Proya grew 1%.
As demand becomes increasingly selective, and derma-brands gain ground, Jefferies’ findings show skin care and color cosmetics accounting for over 80% of China’s beauty market. Both categories initially gave rise to K-beauty.
According to KITA, China’s cosmetic exports reached ₩8.14 trillion (US$6.1 billion) from January to July 2026, up 24% from ₩6.55 trillion (US$4.9 billion) a year earlier. The figures lifted China to fifth in global export rankings, behind France in the lead and South Korea in second place.
In color cosmetics, China has already overtaken Korea. Exports of lip and eye makeup, powders, and nail products totaled ₩1.88 trillion (US$1.41 billion) from January to July, about 2.9 times Korea’s ₩644.7 billion (US$484 million).
From January to July 2026, China’s lip makeup exports were 1.7 times Korea’s, and its eye makeup exports were 3.5 times. China’s exports grew 17% to 33% across all four color cosmetics categories (lip, eye, powders, and nail products), while Korea’s lip makeup and nail product exports fell 15% and 15.6%, respectively. Proya is expanding its international presence with a new research laboratory in France.
According to The Asia Business Daily, Kecia Steelman, CEO of Ulta Beauty, raised C-beauty during the company’s 2026 Q2 fiscal earnings call. She is quoted as saying, “[We are launching] Proya, the number one skin care brand in China. So it’s not just about K-Beauty anymore.”
Proya’s US launch will be the first time a Chinese premium skin care brand joins Ulta’s online and physical networks at the same time. The rollout is planned for November this year, and with it, Proya says it is “moving beyond mere product export to brand globalization.”
To expand, the company says, “brands must not only enter overseas markets but also earn a permanent place in consumers’ daily skin care regimens and secure a voice within elite global beauty narratives.”
Securing that voice, Proya has inaugurated its Europe Innovation Center Laboratory in France, with a 450 square meter site containing 76 pieces of equipment and seven dedicated researchers. The lab will focus on research and innovation in skin longevity, biology, biotechnology, and sustainable ingredients.
The lab will collaborate with the Hangzhou Longwu center in China, which handles formulation, ingredients, safety, and efficacy, and the Shanghai center, which works on hair care and the scalp microbiome.
Proya’s international push comes after its namesake brand, which accounts for around 70% of group revenue, posted a 7% sales decline in H1 2026. The drop was the company’s first after years of uninterrupted growth since its 2017 Shanghai listing. Jefferies says the brand returned to 1% growth in September, but the overseas expansion appears partly aimed at offsetting soft momentum.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Russian data centres in blow to Moscow's AI capabilities
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Russian data centres in blow to Moscow's AI capabilities
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian drones struck five data centres belonging to Russia's largest technology companies in October, causing widespread failures in cloud services, payment systems and navigation apps nationwide.
The Ukrainian armed forces hit three Yandex facilities: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region on 7 October, in Kaluga on 9 October, and in Vladimir on 11 October.
On 14 October a Sber data centre in Balakovo in the Saratov region was struck, and on 18 October a VKontakte data centre in the Leningrad region near St Petersburg came under attack.
Yandex, Sber and VKontakte together run much of Russia's consumer internet infrastructure, from taxi apps and card payment processing to cloud storage and messaging.
None of the companies has disclosed the scale of the damage. Russians have reported persistent difficulties paying for goods, ordering taxis, using navigation services and accessing cloud storage.
Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years, and the strikes have set back Russia's artificial intelligence development, Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society, told AP.
The attacks come as Russia has itself been systematically targeting Ukrainian data centres this autumn.
On 19 October a Russian strike completely destroyed one of the largest facilities of the Ukrainian operator Datagroup in Kyiv, which was declared beyond repair.
The following day a Russian attack damaged Kyiv's GigaCenter. Russia hit several other Ukrainian data centres in September and October.
An earlier Russian strike on a Kyiv data centre in July disrupted internet access, mobile communications and television across the city.
Moscow has targeted Ukraine's IT systems since day one of Russia's full-scale invasion: cruise missiles struck a government server facility on 24 February 2022, and a Russian missile hit the National Data Backup Centre in central Kyiv on 1 March.
Ukraine has since moved most of its data to servers in European countries, limiting the impact of subsequent attacks.
Russian data centres are more vulnerable than Ukrainian ones, analysts say. Under legislation designed to create a so-called "sovereign internet," Russia requires companies to store all data on servers inside the country. That concentration makes the facilities easier to target.
"Russia's problem is that it has to provide air defence over a vast territory, and it does not have enough resources for that," said Nick Reiners, senior geo-technology analyst at Eurasia Group.
"Since all the infrastructure and all the data are located inside Russia, it is relatively easier to disable them." Why air defence systems were not protecting Russian data centres, or failed to do so, has not been explained.
Analysts describe the facilities as soft targets: vast halls filled with servers, power equipment and cooling systems where even a small explosive charge can cause serious damage.
Satellite imagery of the struck Yandex facilities shows fires that may have destroyed microchips and other fragile components.
"After such a strike it is hard to expect anything to have survived: data-centre equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive. Soot from fires is extremely harmful to electronics," Klimarev told AP.
The damage to Yandex is particularly significant for Russia's AI ambitions. The company's three supercomputers, used to develop AI models, rank among the world's top 500. The most powerful, housed in the Sasovo facility, once ranked 19th globally but has since fallen below the top 100.
"Ukrainian drone strikes will probably delay the development of Russian artificial intelligence even further," Connor Martin of the Council on Foreign Relations said. Before the strikes, Russia was already several years behind the US and China.
Restoring the hardware will be complicated by Western sanctions and the global chip shortage. Yandex's supercomputers run on Nvidia A100 processors, which Russia cannot legally import.
Klimarev said the strikes may carry an unintended consequence for Russian internet policy.
"Paradoxically, the attacks on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, because companies will now be forced to move their computing resources, most likely to Europe," he said.
"It is quite likely that many Russian companies are now studying the European market in search of opportunities to rent computing capacity," Klimarev said. He added that Russian authorities might ease their attempts to tighten internet controls to limit the economic damage.
Moscow has for years actively used its IT sector for spying on its users, as well as conduct malign hybrid operations elsewhere.
Under Russia’s SORM legislation, all domestic internet companies including Yandex, VKontakte and Sber are legally required to install FSB backdoors giving the security services access to user data and communications.
These data centres are integrated into Russia’s surveillance apparatus, not purely commercial infrastructure.
VKontakte specifically has been extensively used for state-sponsored propaganda and recruitment. Ukraine banned it in 2017 partly on those grounds.
The Kremlin has demonstrably used AI tools in its disinformation operations, such as rewriting real news articles with pro-Kremlin slants and fabricated claims, publishing them across dozens of sites designed to mimic legitimate international outlets, including Euronews.
It has also used AI-generated video and audio to fabricate statements attributed to Western officials. AI-cloned voices impersonating European politicians have also circulated, though some were detected before they spread widely.
More recently, it has flooded the internet with repetitive pro-Kremlin content to skew what AI chatbots retrieve and eventually how they are trained. NewsGuard stress tests found chatbots repeated false claims in roughly a third of responses when prompted adversarially.
Researchers at the Carnegie Endowment have however stated that training-data poisoning is slow, heavily filtered and increasingly countered by behavioural rules built into newer models.
EU sanctions prohibit the supply of IT services, software and cloud capacity to Russian companies.
Firms seeking to circumvent the restrictions have used intermediaries, anonymous hosting providers or foreign corporate structures. Brussels has been tightening enforcement of those rules.

articles.title_orig: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.title_zh: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: Documents show German party’s scramble to request support after president’s 2016 election win and co-leader’s pursuit of Steve Bannon
A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote , came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8% , and now leads national polls at about 30% . In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation , and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist .
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme . Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader, Alice Weidel, and the key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe” .
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, the then chancellor, Angela Merkel, offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister, Ursula von der Leyen, called the result a “ huge shock ”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance . On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic , and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down .
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. articles.title_orig: People are fixing their TV OSes with Claude
articles.title_zh: People are fixing their TV OSes with Claude
articles.content_orig:
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Vibe coding has reached TVs. Social media is awash with posts from people using LLMs and open-source tools to remove ads and tracking, trim bloat so the OS runs faster, and even completely change the look and organization of their homescreens. While a lot of it is fun — one user turned their TV homescreen into a Pokémon town — I think there’s a level of frustration behind it, too. And TV companies should take notice.
Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox , and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things — remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you’re watching — without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV’s built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokémon one below.
Most of the projects we’ve seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don’t require root access or firmware hacking, and they’re reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android’s ability to install custom launchers — in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.
As Verge friend Chris Person notes in his Aftermath post , none of this requires AI. These projects take advantage of capabilities that already exist in Android, and in some cases reinvent the wheel. Android debloating programs that use ADB have been around for years, and so have replacement launchers that make Google TV OS look like Apple TV . AI just made the process easier and faster.
There’s nothing similar available for Samsung’s Tizen OS or LG’s webOS, apart from rooting the TV, which is a whole different level of hacking and device control. While there’s a webOS vibe hack for LG TVs that’s based on cleanyourtv, it doesn’t really do the same thing, essentially streaming the Apple TV-like launcher from an always-on device on the same network. They also won’t work for Roku or Vizio’s SmartCast.
These projects, or any OS vibe coding someone might attempt, won’t necessarily stop all data collection. A good basic rule is that if the TV is connected to the internet, it’s collected at least some data. Dumbtv blocks certain manufacturer and ad partner addresses your TV sends data to, but since it’s usually encrypted during transit, knowing what exactly gets sent is impossible. The data blocking is similar to what you can do with Pi-hole to block malicious DNS requests on your network.
TVs have increasingly become a means for companies to gather viewing data and serve up ads. By using automatic content recognition (ACR) and digital fingerprinting, manufacturers are able to know what content you’re watching, send that information to their ad partners, and then display targeted ads on the TV.
ACR isn’t just used for ads, though. It allows companies to measure audience metrics, and it can feed show recommendations based on what you’ve watched. It’s important to note that users need to agree to ACR tracking, and there are ways to opt out of it after the fact in a TV’s menus (although those options are not always easy to find). There are also options in most menus — again, usually buried — for turning off targeted ads.
But even after doing that, there’s always concern that companies still collect some amount of your data and use it in ways you might not be comfortable with. Whether or not it’s true does little to assuage those fears. The weekend of vibe coding, on the other hand, is a way for people to try and take control of their TVs to get the user experience they want.
There are also dangers to vibe-coding your TV. One person who tried to vibe-hack a Samsung TV with Claude bricked it. The only way to fully avoid ACR, ads, or any type of data collection is to never connect it to the internet. A firmware download to a USB stick can apply critical updates instead of Wi-Fi or Ethernet. If you still want to stream content, a streaming device that doesn’t use ACR , like an Apple TV 4K (grab a last-generation model before the expensive new one replaces it), is an option. But any streaming requires sharing some amount of your data with someone to function properly.
The biggest takeaway from the vibe-coding weekend is that the current state of TV OSes has people fed up. Most people aren’t going to stop watching TV anytime soon, but the experience needs to improve. The ads, the data collection, and the cluttered layouts are too aggravating. AI now allows anyone to code their own solution, and it’s only going to get easier. If TV manufacturers don’t take note and make changes, there’s a chance that users will make the changes for them.

articles.title_orig: All lanes open after deadly crash in Durham creates severe delays on I-40, I-885 near RDU
articles.title_zh: All lanes open after deadly crash in Durham creates severe delays on I-40, I-885 near RDU
articles.content_orig:
A busy stretch of Interstate 40 East near Raleigh-Durham International Airport reopened Friday morning several hours after Durham police found a woman who was hit by multiple unknown vehicles.
Durham police said they responded to a call about a pedestrian being hit on I-40 near Davis Drive around 1:30 a.m. When they arrived, they found the woman dead and said she had been hit multiple times by unknown vehicles.
The eastbound lanes of I-40 were closed for a mile from Exit 280 at Davis Drive to Exit 281 to South Miami Boulevard. The severe delays extended onto Interstate 885 as well.
At 8 a.m., a lane had reopened on I-40 and traffic was flowing again. All lanes on I-40 reopened by 8:30 a.m.
Hours before the morning commute, WRAL Breaking News Tracker arrived before 4 a.m. to find multiple officers blocking the interstate for an investigation. Police would not let reporters near the scene.
WRAL's Shaun Gallagher arrived at 6 a.m. as the backup worsened. According to Gallagher, the miles of backups on the road resembled 8:30 a.m. rush hour instead of the usual 6 a.m. traffic.
Sky 5 flew over the delays at 7:15 a.m., showing miles and miles of traffic.
Police said they cannot release any other information about the investigation at this time.

articles.title_orig: Ambush of Salvadoran Soldiers Escalates Haiti’s Anti-Gang Mission
articles.title_zh: Ambush of Salvadoran Soldiers Escalates Haiti’s Anti-Gang Mission
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador has deployed troops to Haiti to try to rescue four Salvadoran service members believed to have been captured by Haitian gangs, according to a spokesperson for the UN-authorized multinational security mission in Haiti known as the Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The missing service members, described as non-combatant aviation technicians that were supporting the GSF mission, were ambushed by gangs on October 18, Salvadoran officials have said.
The GSF has been carrying out a dayslong operation to try to find them. The effort has resulted in armed clashes that have left at least seven gang members dead and four GSF personnel wounded, the GSF has said.
A spokesperson for the security mission confirmed to CNN on Thursday Salvadoran troops had arrived in Haiti to support the effort.
The Miami Herald first reported that a 100-strong team was deployed. El Salvador has not commented on the specific details of the mission.
It comes a day after Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele announced that his country had launched an unspecified “military operation” to rescue the missing men.
Bukele, who has carried out a brutal crackdown on gangs in his own country, warned Haitian gang members that they would face a more severe response if they didn’t release the service members alive.
“And do not take our word for empty threats. We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he said on X.
Gang leader Lanmo Sanjou issued a response to Bukele on Thursday, filming himself with large quantities of ammunition and warning that his group would “fight to stay alive.”
The GSF was established by the UN Security Council in 2025 to help Haiti fight the gangs plaguing the country . According to the resolution adopted at that time, the force consists of 5,500 military or police personnel and 50 civilians from various nations. El Salvador is one of the countries that agreed to provide personnel. Bukele says their primary job is to carry out medical evacuations.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.title_zh: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.content_orig:
Shares of South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix closed higher on Friday, reversing losses of as much as 3% earlier in the session after the company's decision to halt a review of a potential U.S. initial public offering for its subsidiary Solidigm.
The stock reversed earlier losses to close 4.4% higher.
Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the stock's rebound suggested that concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had been weighing on investor sentiment.
"SK Hynix shareholders have got the outcome they were pushing for," Gilbert said, adding that "in the short term, it removes a governance worry and keeps Solidigm's value inside the company."
He explained that SK Hynix faces the challenge of funding Solidigm's growth without compromising share buybacks and dividends, as the company needs to demonstrate a credible funding plan as it prepares to report earnings next week.
"Solidigm will halt its review of potential pre-IPO and IPO options," the company said in the statement after assessing recent capital market conditions and share price trends, while also exploring various funding options to finance a new U.S. semiconductor fabrication plant amid growing demand for AI memory.
The chip manufacturer said an IPO could have helped fund Solidigm's expansion while providing greater financial flexibility for shareholder returns, including dividends, share buybacks and share cancellations.
However, financial market volatility had increased and contributed to a broader correction in semiconductor stocks, prompting SK Hynix to reassess whether an IPO would benefit existing shareholders.
SK Hynix said that Solidigm's existing production facilities had limited capacity to meet rising AI-driven memory demand, underscoring the need for additional manufacturing capacity in the U.S.
The decision also follows regulatory scrutiny in South Korea.
The country's financial regulator said Monday that a potential U.S. listing of Solidigm could violate South Korean rules restricting dual listings, according to Reuters.
Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin said regulators were examining whether the IPO would require a review under the country's rules designed to protect minority shareholders.
SK Hynix said Solidigm's investment needs remain unchanged and that it would continue exploring alternative financing options to support the subsidiary's growth and enhance shareholder value.
The announcement comes as U.S. technology stocks face pressure amid worries over AI spending.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 2.6% on Thursday, its worst session since June, while Nvidia fell 4.4% and Advanced Micro Devices dropped 8.1%.
Amid a sell-off in memory stocks, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that he does not expect an oversupply of memory chips by 2029, despite concerns over weakening demand.
AI data center stocks have also come under pressure amid growing concerns over financing risks and the pace of AI infrastructure expansion. Shares of CoreWeave plunged 10% on Thursday, extending their monthly decline to 36%, while Australia's NextDC tumbled nearly 40% on Wednesday after cutting its earnings forecast.

articles.title_orig: Samsung is releasing a new foldable next week, and it just leaked
articles.title_zh: Samsung is releasing a new foldable next week, and it just leaked
articles.content_orig:
The upcoming Samsung W27 could be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and boast the same specifications, but in a more luxurious body and with a more premium asking price
Samsung's ultra-premium, limited-edition W series foldables are offered in the Chinese market. This time, the brand is working on the W27, which could be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.
A recently surfaced image courtesy of Ice Universe on X gives us an early glimpse of the alleged Samsung W27. The leaked photo showcases the foldable smartphone sporting a dark blue finish highlighted by golden accents surrounding the rear camera island.
Talking about specifications, for reference, the Samsung W25 and W26 were just more luxurious aesthetic rebrands of the Galaxy Z Fold 6 Special Edition and Galaxy Z Fold 7 , respectively. The core specs between these devices remained the same. Going by that, we expect the W27 to pack similar specs to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra .
For starters, it could be powered by the same Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset . The upcoming Samsung foldable may also use the same 200 MP cameras and internal displays, but all in a slightly more luxurious-looking body.
Besides the phone itself, the main selling point of the W series is also its packaging elements. With a custom box, the phone is expected to be offered in its own custom case, power adapter and card of authenticity, which collectors will appreciate.
As for the Samsung W27 pricing, we expect it to be pricier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's Rs 1,99,999 price tag. This is because even the W26 launched at 16,999 Chinese yuan (approx. Rs 2,41,500) in China, which is significantly pricier than the Galaxy Z Fold 7's Rs 1,74,999 price tag in India.
Samsung has yet to announce an official launch date for the W27. However, replying to one of the comments, Ice Universe said the launch date is set for October 29, 2026 . This makes sense since Samsung's previous W series foldables launched in the October to November timeframe.
Another thing to note is that, since Samsung's W series is exclusive to China, we don't really have hopes for it to make it to India.

articles.title_orig: Apple’s $2,000 foldable iPhone hits stores. Is it worth it?
articles.title_zh: Apple’s $2,000 foldable iPhone hits stores. Is it worth it?
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s first foldable iPhone sparked a launch-day circus in New York on Friday, with fans lining up for hours — and in some cases overnight — before stores opened, only to find some flagship locations were already out of walk-in stock by mid-morning.
At Apple’s glass-cube Fifth Avenue store, a video posted online showed a “massive queue” around 4:15 a.m. as customers waited for the new iPhone Duo.
By 10 a.m. , a Reddit user posted that the store had “ran out of stock for walk-ins,” adding that the remaining line was made up of customers with confirmed pickup orders.
The frenzy began well before dawn.
One launch-day customer, Alex Wong, told The US Sun he got in line at 2 p.m. Thursday — a full 18 hours before the Fifth Avenue store’s 8 a.m. opening — and was still only around 25th in line.
Elsewhere in the city, crowds and inventory varied sharply from store to store, underscoring just how uneven Apple’s launch-day supply appeared to be.
At the World Trade Center store, one Reddit user wrote that employees came out at 6 a.m. to start processing orders and that there were “probably 200 people in line.”
The same poster complained: “Many scalpers. Many ordering 2, don’t even know what they’re ordering.”
Another poster at the same location estimated the crowd at “maybe 130 people” and said store staff had warned shoppers there were “very few units” available.
At Apple’s Upper East Side location, a Reddit user summed up the mood more bluntly: “Apple UES NYC — sold out for walk-ins 😓.”
iPhone Duo Apple Store Camp Out in Los Angeles! #iPhoneDuo #Apple pic.twitter.com/LiUbndlwY4
Downtown Brooklyn offered a slightly different picture. One earlier post estimated about 50 people were outside , while another shopper later reported: “WAITED IN LINE, THEY JUST GOT STOCK. ONLY BLUE AS OF 9:18 AM.”
The run on the Duo comes after Apple warned that walk-in quantities at US stores would be limited on launch day.
The social media chatter suggests the scarcity only added to the hype.
In Chicago, one buyer said he arrived 45 minutes before opening and still managed to reserve a 512GB “Night Sky” model.
In Dallas, another said showing up 30 minutes before doors opened was enough to land the configuration he wanted.
An Apple user in Dallas said he waited 11 hours outside Apple’s University Park store to score a white 512GB iPhone Duo.
But in Ardmore, Penn., just outside of Philadelphia, one shopper said he arrived at 5:45 a.m. and the store was “Sold out 7:30ish.”
The same shopper reported that Apple’s King of Prussia, Penn., location sold out shortly after 8 a.m., while nearby Willow Grove Park had also run out by the time he arrived around 9 a.m.
JUST IN – Video shows a massive queue outside Apple Fifth Avenue in New York around 4:15 AM as customers line up for the iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/jkLUJyz8mM
He complained about entire families purchasing two phones apiece, including parents who brought babies in strollers and carriers into the chilly morning air.
“[S]calpers suck,” he fumed, adding that he planned to console himself with ice cream while waiting until December for his phone.
At Delaware’s Christiana Mall, another shopper estimated that 200 to 300 people were lined up for the new gadget.
In Orlando, Apple’s store at the Mall at Millenia stopped accepting walk-in orders by about 8:15 a.m., according to a Reddit user who reported that security guards had been stationed throughout the queue and at the cutoff point.
This was the line-before-the-line. 4:15am in Las Vegas (Town Square) with 30-40 people. Now, probably 150+ and I can no longer see the end of the line. pic.twitter.com/r5oeLLo3iw
In Colorado, some would-be customers weren’t even allowed to camp out.
One Reddit user said mall security kicked early shoppers out of Denver’s Cherry Creek location and barred them from lining up until 7 a.m. The customer subsequently headed to another Apple store in Colorado Springs.
Meanwhile, in Las Vegas, a social media user reported that the crowd outside Apple’s Town Square store swelled from an estimated 30 to 40 people at 4:15 a.m. to more than 150 later in the morning.
In Boise, Idaho, a shopper who arrived at 4:45 a.m. said he was 19th in line and managed to purchase a Duo.
The store subsequently sold out, with an estimated 50 to 60 early customers getting phones while later arrivals were turned away.
And in Los Angeles, the launch produced dramatically different outcomes depending on the store.
One shopper at Manhattan Village in Manhattan Beach reported that roughly 50 people lined up and everyone managed to get a phone.
But another Reddit user reported that Apple’s Century City location had already sold out.

Cheryl Cassoni reports on President Trump's threat to halt Canadian airplane maker Bombardier's sales to the US. Vogel Group's Samir Kapadia analyzes the trade pressure campaign and its political stakes in battleground states.
FIRST ON FOX: Canadian jetmaker Bombardier announced Friday it is "expanding in America" and "creating thousands of jobs" as part of a $270 million investment deal touted by President Donald Trump.
The development comes after Trump said in September that Bombardier should no longer be allowed to sell its planes in the United States unless it manufactures them domestically.
"Bombardier is expanding its presence across the country, hiring 800 people for jobs located in its home base of Kansas as well as Texas, Indiana, and Connecticut," the company said Friday in a press release obtained by FOX Business. "This strategy includes an initial phase of investment estimated at $270M earmarked for infrastructure growth."
"Our American service network is a key pillar of Bombardier's growth strategy. This new wave of expansion and hiring reflects our long-term confidence in this market and our employees in America," said Eric Martel, president and CEO of Bombardier.
TRUMP TARGETS BOMBARDIER, SAYS CANADIAN JETMAKER 'MUST BUILD' IN THE US
Canadian jetmaker Bombardier said Friday that it is "continuing to significantly enhance its American footprint." (Bombardier)
"Based on our constructive conversations with the U.S. administration, we see a bright path forward for our highly skilled aerospace workers as well as a positive environment for Bombardier to continue pursuing direct investments to grow our American footprint," he added.
The company said it is "actively recruiting for 500 positions across the country and plans to create an additional 300 jobs through footprint expansion projects," and that "Texas is planned to be the next pillar of expansion and will account for 150 of the 300 new jobs."
"Hiring activities will further be spread across the company’s U.S. home base in Kansas as well as in Indiana and Connecticut," the company continued.
GOP SENATOR UNVEILS PLAN TO EXPAND TRUMP ACCOUNTS TO PEOPLE UNDER 40: 'GAME-CHANGER'
President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a midterm rally at Truist Arena on the Northern Kentucky University campus on Oct. 17, 2026 in Highland Heights, Ky. (Eric Lee/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas has done an incredible job in representing his Great State!" Trump said on Truth Social late Thursday while revealing the investment. "Companies are coming to America, investing BILLIONS OF DOLLARS, and creating JOBS like never before."
Bombardier said its Learning Center in Wichita, Kansas "represents one component of Bombardier’s broader investment in this iconic city."
"Inaugurated last week, the new North American Learning Center reinforces the company’s commitment to developing talent, enhancing capabilities and supporting the long-term growth of its Kansas operations," according to the company.
"Bombardier’s newest American service facility at Fort Wayne International Airport in Fort Wayne, Indiana, is an approximately 64,500-square-foot facility that will accommodate up to six aircraft and offer scheduled and unscheduled maintenance, modifications, avionics installations and AOG [aircraft on ground] support. articles.title_orig: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.title_zh: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.content_orig:
The appeal of local AI is obvious enough. Local AI models are free and don't incur any costs, usage-based or otherwise. They work offline. They're private, as your data is never shared with Big Tech, Big AI, or their partners. And they can be incredibly efficient, though the most efficient models that work with your computer's NPU are less common than those that rely on power-hungry GPUs like those found in RTX Spark computers.
But local AI is still more promise than reality because the models are much smaller and much less capable than cloud-based frontier models. AI evolves quickly, of course, and local AI benefits from this rapid progress too. But it's important to correctly frame the relative capabilities. That is, while local AI will never "close the gap" with cloud-based AI, it will be good enough depending on the use case.
This is the point behind hybrid AI, or what Microsoft calls Hybrid Intelligence: Use local AI as much as possible and only hand off tasks to cloud-based AI when required. In time, we hope, local AI will be good enough for enough tasks that cloud AI is rarely if ever needed.
It's a nice dream. But that's all it is today if you use AI to get real work done.
For one thing, hybrid AI requires a capable orchestrator, and we don't even have basic orchestrators for the most part right now. Microsoft is working to bring hybrid AI orchestration to tools like the GitHub Copilot app and even Copilot in Windows 11. And other Big Tech and Big AI companies--from Google to Anthropic and OpenAI and others--will no doubt roll out hybrid AI orchestration capabilities into their AI front-ends too. But that's not available today, certainly not broadly or in any mainstream AI assistant.
And that means we're stuck with a choice. We can use cloud AI, as we have been for the past three and a half years through whatever AI assistant or other AI front-end, incurring usage-based costs as we go and with the need to be online for the duration. Or we can suck it up and experiment with local AI. Which requires a lot of know-how, the right hardware, and unfamiliar tools. Copilot+ PC got it right It shouldn't be that way. If you're familiar with Copilot+ PCs, which I think of as the second-generation AI PCs, you may recall Microsoft claiming two and a half years ago that these new PCs shipped with over 40 so-called small language models (SLMs), which are smaller local AI models that, in this case, are each optimized for specific use cases. And if you use a Copilot+ PC, you might know that these models all need to be updated just like any other software, and that some need to be downloaded before specific features in individual apps will even work. For example, before you can use the Copilot+ PC-specific features in Microsoft Paint, you're prompted to download and install an Image Generation model from the Microsoft Store.
Say what you will about Copilot+ PCs, but this platform's local AI features are aimed at mainstream users...

articles.title_orig: Oil price rises above $115 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
articles.title_zh: Oil price rises above $115 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
articles.content_orig:
Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.
The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran .
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”

Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

articles.title_zh: Where to Buy iPhone Duo Today: Stores, Pickup, and Wait Times
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s first foldable iPhone sparked a launch-day circus in New York on Friday, with fans lining up for hours — and in some cases overnight — before stores opened, only to find some flagship locations were already out of walk-in stock by mid-morning.
At Apple’s glass-cube Fifth Avenue store, a video posted online showed a “massive queue” around 4:15 a.m. as customers waited for the new iPhone Duo.
By 10 a.m. , a Reddit user posted that the store had “ran out of stock for walk-ins,” adding that the remaining line was made up of customers with confirmed pickup orders.
The frenzy began well before dawn.
One launch-day customer, Alex Wong, told The US Sun he got in line at 2 p.m. Thursday — a full 18 hours before the Fifth Avenue store’s 8 a.m. opening — and was still only around 25th in line.
Elsewhere in the city, crowds and inventory varied sharply from store to store, underscoring just how uneven Apple’s launch-day supply appeared to be.
At the World Trade Center store, one Reddit user wrote that employees came out at 6 a.m. to start processing orders and that there were “probably 200 people in line.”
The same poster complained: “Many scalpers. Many ordering 2, don’t even know what they’re ordering.”
Another poster at the same location estimated the crowd at “maybe 130 people” and said store staff had warned shoppers there were “very few units” available.
At Apple’s Upper East Side location, a Reddit user summed up the mood more bluntly: “Apple UES NYC — sold out for walk-ins 😓.”
iPhone Duo Apple Store Camp Out in Los Angeles! #iPhoneDuo #Apple pic.twitter.com/LiUbndlwY4
Downtown Brooklyn offered a slightly different picture. One earlier post estimated about 50 people were outside , while another shopper later reported: “WAITED IN LINE, THEY JUST GOT STOCK. ONLY BLUE AS OF 9:18 AM.”
The run on the Duo comes after Apple warned that walk-in quantities at US stores would be limited on launch day.
The social media chatter suggests the scarcity only added to the hype.
In Chicago, one buyer said he arrived 45 minutes before opening and still managed to reserve a 512GB “Night Sky” model.
In Dallas, another said showing up 30 minutes before doors opened was enough to land the configuration he wanted.
An Apple user in Dallas said he waited 11 hours outside Apple’s University Park store to score a white 512GB iPhone Duo.
But in Ardmore, Penn., just outside of Philadelphia, one shopper said he arrived at 5:45 a.m. and the store was “Sold out 7:30ish.”
The same shopper reported that Apple’s King of Prussia, Penn., location sold out shortly after 8 a.m., while nearby Willow Grove Park had also run out by the time he arrived around 9 a.m.
JUST IN – Video shows a massive queue outside Apple Fifth Avenue in New York around 4:15 AM as customers line up for the iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/jkLUJyz8mM
He complained about entire families purchasing two phones apiece, including parents who brought babies in strollers and carriers into the chilly morning air.
“[S]calpers suck,” he fumed, adding that he planned to console himself with ice cream while waiting until December for his phone.
At Delaware’s Christiana Mall, another shopper estimated that 200 to 300 people were lined up for the new gadget.
In Orlando, Apple’s store at the Mall at Millenia stopped accepting walk-in orders by about 8:15 a.m., according to a Reddit user who reported that security guards had been stationed throughout the queue and at the cutoff point.
This was the line-before-the-line. 4:15am in Las Vegas (Town Square) with 30-40 people. Now, probably 150+ and I can no longer see the end of the line. pic.twitter.com/r5oeLLo3iw
In Colorado, some would-be customers weren’t even allowed to camp out.
One Reddit user said mall security kicked early shoppers out of Denver’s Cherry Creek location and barred them from lining up until 7 a.m. The customer subsequently headed to another Apple store in Colorado Springs.
Meanwhile, in Las Vegas, a social media user reported that the crowd outside Apple’s Town Square store swelled from an estimated 30 to 40 people at 4:15 a.m. to more than 150 later in the morning.
In Boise, Idaho, a shopper who arrived at 4:45 a.m. said he was 19th in line and managed to purchase a Duo.
The store subsequently sold out, with an estimated 50 to 60 early customers getting phones while later arrivals were turned away.
And in Los Angeles, the launch produced dramatically different outcomes depending on the store.
One shopper at Manhattan Village in Manhattan Beach reported that roughly 50 people lined up and everyone managed to get a phone.
But another Reddit user reported that Apple’s Century City location had already sold out.

articles.title_orig: Could Europe’s cost-of-living protests sharpen EU-China trade tensions?
articles.title_zh: Could Europe’s cost-of-living protests sharpen EU-China trade tensions?
articles.content_orig:
Unrest over economic hardship could strengthen calls to protect industry and jobs, though direct impact on trade talks is uncertain
As violent protests fuelled partly by the cost-of-living crisis shake parts of Europe, most notably France, analysts say the unrest could add to pressure on European policymakers to take a tougher trade stance towards China.
“One could argue that the EU looks weaker, but then one could also argue that there is more of a need to show external strength at a time of such events,” said David Henig, director of the UK Trade Policy Project at the European Centre for International Political Economy.
On Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron said requests to hold protests submitted by people “with no legitimacy” would be banned in the coming days. Requests filed by unions would be examined under the law, while local authorities would propose alternative routes to keep demonstrations away from city centres, he said.

articles.title_orig: What smart people are saying about AI unleashing an online 'vulnerability tsunami'
articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about AI unleashing an online 'vulnerability tsunami'
articles.content_orig:
It's been a nightmarish week for cybersecurity.
AI helped discover two "critical" flaws in the infrastructure of PHP , a programming language that up to 70% of websites use, prompting companies to race to roll out a fix or risk being hacked.
The incident has illustrated how AI is creating a new level of risk for businesses and consumers online, in a week when multiple other cyber threats caused headaches for security workers.
Here's what executives and analysts are saying about the biggest cyber threat of the moment — and how AI could make things even worse.
Anthropic's deputy security chief, Jason Clinton, warns that a "vulnerability tsunami" is coming — and says critical infrastructure hasn't caught up.
Clinton posted on X on Wednesday about the need to "patch critical infrastructure" before core network vulnerabilities get exploited. On Thursday, he issued another warning to companies.
"As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better," he wrote.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)," he added.
Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, weighed in on several cybersecurity threats from Wednesday to Thursday.
"Regarding potential attacks on energy, food, and water infrastructure, the threat is quite real. Someone is currently probing infra and feeling it out, it is an active threat. Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case," Curran wrote on Wednesday in response to an NSA cybersecurity advisory about threat actors.
On Thursday, Curran also highlighted a hack of Quest Diagnostics, which he said serves "roughly half" of the US's hospitals and physicians.
In February, Matt Shumer, the former CEO of Hyperwrite, published a viral essay on his website titled "Something Big Is Happening," in which he warned of large-scale disruptions wrought by AI that could upend the world order.
Shumer published another essay on Thursday on his website and LinkedIn, this time titled "The Internet Is Under Attack. Here's How to Protect Yourself and Your Family."
"Right now, as you read this, swarms of AI agents are likely trying to break into the websites you use. Not one of them. Many of them," Shumer wrote. "We are in the middle of the biggest cybersecurity moment in years."
This is what could happen, per Shumer's post:
Shumer also outlined four ways people can protect themselves, including updating all their software and staying off sites they're unfamiliar with while companies and websites alike make their security updates.
He also advises that people protect their bank accounts by being extra cautious about any and all codes and links that they receive. People should also "close the doors you aren't using" by unplugging smart gadgets and deleting apps that aren't being utilized.
"Every connected thing is another way in," Shumer wrote.
Marc Benioff agreed with Anthropic's Jason Clinton in an X post on Thursday.
"Jason is 100% right. Code red," Benioff wrote, along with a red alarm emoji.
Sriram Krishnan, a prominent venture capitalist and former senior AI policy advisor for President Donald Trump, said that the PHP vulnerabilities are a "harbinger of things to come" as AI models continue to detect long-standing cyber issues.
"However the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes," he said in a post on X.
The new cyber reality may require more public-private partnerships to build the required infrastructure, he said.
The Menlo Venture partner Deedy Das warned that "the era of vibe hacking is here" in a series of posts on X.
He said he'd seen firsthand that "even non-technical people" can exploit common vulnerabilities, such as PHP, using AI models. Das said someone could theoretically direct certain models to any website and instruct them to quickly locate the vulnerabilities.
"Once you figure it out, it is downright trivial to do. The digital infrastructure of the world is at risk," he wrote.
AI agents have ended the era of "security through obscurity" because they can devote once-unthinkable time and effort to finding vulnerabilities, Box CEO Aaron Levie said on X. People will need to upgrade legacy infrastructure, modernize security policies, and tighten access controls, among other measures, he said.
"Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors," Levie wrote.
Yet Levie thinks humans also have an important role to play in the cyber revolution — he predicted a boom in cybersecurity jobs , which could become a huge investment area for companies.
"You will need more talent to point the agents at the most critical work, review findings, patch systems, respond to incidents, and more," he said.

articles.title_orig: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.title_zh: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.content_orig:
Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.
The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.
A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

articles.title_orig: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.title_zh: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.content_orig:
The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world, including those of major companies and national governments. The PHP Foundation released two patches designed to fix the vulnerabilities. Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images hide caption
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.
OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.
The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.
"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.
As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.
Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.
In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."
Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.
"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

articles.title_zh: Japan university defence bids surge as post-war taboo fades amid China concerns
articles.content_orig:
Changing security norms and cash shortages push Japanese researchers to pursue state-funded defence tech projects
Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defence capabilities.
The increase is the clearest sign yet that academia’s decades-long resistance to military-linked work is diminishing.
The bids accounted for more than half the record 560 applications received by the ministry this year, up from 340 last year, with the rest coming from public research institutes and companies.
Of the 47 projects selected for funding under the 12.9 billion yen (US$82 million) programme, 30 will be led by university researchers, with 11 universities – including Osaka, Nagoya and Keio – winning grants for the first time.

articles.title_orig: Treasuries’ AI Link Shows Sharp Shift as Haven Trade Returns
articles.title_zh: Treasuries’ AI Link Shows Sharp Shift as Haven Trade Returns
articles.content_orig:
Investors ran for cover this week as artificial intelligence fears hit stocks, driving the 10-year Treasury below 5%.
The benchmark yield stayed below 5% on Friday, after falling beneath that level Thursday for the first time in a month, as investors continued to express misgivings over the massive debt being taken on by technology companies to finance their build out of AI networks. Tech stocks sank, bond yields on outstanding tech debt rose and spreads on credit default swaps widened in a host of AI companies.
"The selloff in tech stocks drove the flight-to-quality bid, compounded by continued weakness in the French sovereign market," BMO's credit strategy team said in a note Friday. "Interestingly, the focus on weakness in the equity market ... [has] overshadowed the move in the energy market, with Treasuries rallying despite WTI crude oil testing $100/bbl."
On Friday, yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose by 1 basis point to 4.966%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve policy, increased by 2 basis points to 4.658%. Yields on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which react to geopolitical developments — were relatively flat at 5.292%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The bounce back in Treasury prices comes just weeks after 10- and 30-year yields jumped to their highest levels in more than 20 years .
Since that time, concerns have grown about the billions being spent by tech companies. CoreWeave has led the rout, losing 10% on Thursday and 36% in October. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 stands at 15.72%, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is 1,138. Any reading above 1,000 is generally considered distressed.
Next week, the focus will turn to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, due on Wednesday. The market doesn't expect the central bank to raise rates this month, but is pricing in a roughly 72% probability of a quarter percentage point hike in December, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool .
"At this stage, the tightening of financial conditions hasn't been dramatic enough to preclude another rate hike this year, although a sustained deterioration could readily alter the Fed's policy calculus," BMO Capital said.
Traders are awaiting Friday's flash S&P Global PMI readings on manufacturing and services for a fresh view on U.S. growth and inflation. Meanwhile, rising energy costs continue to weigh on the inflation outlook.
West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery climbed another 1.6% to $101.10 a barrel on Friday, while Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, traded 1.4% higher, at $114.71 a barrel.
Firmer energy prices come as fresh attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabian oil installations drove new fears over an oil supply squeeze. Reports earlier this week suggested that the U.S. and Israel could resume strikes against Iran following the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
